problem: Conventional VLN agents are trained in disturbance-free environments and fail under route deviations caused by obstacles, interruptions or wrong actions; robustness has been largely ignored in VLN.
motivation: Real-world disturbances vary in form but usually cause a route deviation, and even disturbance-free navigation deviates through wrong actions. Training an agent to still reach the goal by following the original instruction after a deviation should improve both robustness and general performance.
key_idea: Impose route deviations by deleting edges in the navigation graph, introduce the perturbed trajectories progressively as the agent matches GT trajectories, and use perturbation-aware contrastive learning to separate perturbation-free and perturbation-based trajectory encodings.
insight: Perturbed trajectories act as useful augmentation data: Fig. shows SPL rises with the perturbed-data proportion, and the proportion rises with SPL. On EnvDropout R2R val-unseen, progressive augmentation beats the non-progressive one (SR 50.4 vs 49.2), and contrastive learning adds more (51.3). Without PROPER, perturbation costs about 20 SR/SPL points on PP-R2R (VLN-BERT val-unseen SR 61.5 to 38.8).
method: Perturbation via edge deletion: delete edge (c_t,c_{t+1}) on the connectivity graph so the agent must choose an alternative action a'_t. Deletable edges are precomputed (Algorithm 1) so that start-goal reachability is preserved. The alternative node must lie within distance r (the scene's average neighbor distance) of the original node.

Perturbation-aware GT trajectory: p_obs = p(s,c_t) + shortest detour p(c_t,m) + p(m,d), where m lies on the remaining GT path and the perturbed edge is excluded. The detour is minimal, so the original instruction is reused.

Progressive perturbed trajectory augmentation: train first on perturbation-free data. At each iteration, perturb the newly GT-matched (partially or fully overlapping) rollouts and accumulate them with earlier perturbed trajectories. The new action is sampled with the original prediction masked.

Perturbation-aware contrastive learning: the trajectory encoding is the final decoder hidden state. In perturbation-free scenes e_f has positive e_g, intra-negatives e_og (all perturbation-aware GTs) and inter-negatives e_m (the minibatch). In perturbation-based scenes e_p has positive e_og, intra-negatives e_og' (other perturbation positions) and e_m. Both use InfoNCE (L_f, L_p).
Objective: L = L_RL + 0.2 L_IL + 1·L_f + 1·L_p. The paradigm is model-agnostic and is plugged into EnvDropout, RelGraph and VLN-BERT with the same schedules.
PP-R2R benchmark: R2R trajectories that admit perturbation (4,623 train / 335 val-seen / 769 val-unseen) with perturbation-aware GT paths, used to evaluate deviation robustness.

setting.backbone: EnvDropout (LSTM seq2seq), RelGraph (graph-based), VLN-BERT (Transformer), each trained with PROPER
setting.training_data: R2R train plus the baselines' augmented instruction-path pairs, with perturbed trajectories generated online; CVDN for the generalization test; no extra web data
setting.privileged: none at test time (perturbation is applied only in the perturbation-based evaluation, PP-R2R)

numbers.extra: single run; uses the baseline's augmented data

numbers_note: R2R values are printed as integers in the table. Only the main variants are listed; ablation numbers (e.g., EnvDropout val-unseen SR 51.3 NE 5.13 in the ablation table) are not entered as separate rows.
results: PROPER improves three baselines on R2R in perturbation-free settings (e.g. EnvDropout val-unseen SR 52→55; VLN-BERT val-unseen SR 63→64, SPL 57→58; test-unseen SPL 57→58). On PP-R2R it recovers a large part of the perturbation-induced drop (VLN-BERT val-unseen SR 38.8→42.9, EnvDropout 23.9→30.3), but remains far below perturbation-free performance (61.5 for VLN-BERT).
limitations: The perturbation is only a graph edge deletion in discrete R2R, with no real obstacles or visual changes, and is evaluated only on R2R/PP-R2R/CVDN.
Gains on perturbation-free R2R are small (1-3 SR points), and the drop under perturbation stays large even after training.
Visual ambiguity, such as two similar doors, still causes failures, and there are no real-robot tests.
